opus-5.5.text:
I think the key thing is that once AI systems can do AI research themselves, you remove the main bottleneck we've had, which is the number of skilled human researchers. Right now there are maybe a few thousand people who can meaningfully push the frontier. If you can spin up the equivalent of tens or hundreds of thousands of top researchers, running faster than humans, working around the clock, and sharing what they learn instantly, then progress that might have taken a decade could get compressed into a year or less.

A few factors would make that especially explosive. First, copyability. Once you have one system that's as good as a top researcher, you don't need to train another; you just run more copies, limited mainly by compute. Second, speed. These systems can think and write code much faster than we can, so the cycle of forming a hypothesis, running an experiment, and analyzing results gets much shorter. Third, the improvements compound. Better algorithms make the next generation of models more capable, those models find further algorithmic improvements, and so on. You don't necessarily need more hardware for a while, because there's a lot of slack in algorithmic efficiency.

There are some brakes. Compute is a real constraint, since experiments still need GPUs, and some research requires running large training runs that take time. But even with fixed hardware, if algorithmic efficiency keeps doubling quickly, you could go from roughly human-level to far beyond it in a short window.

What worries me is less the raw speed than what it does to oversight. If the loop is mostly automated, humans become a bottleneck that labs feel pressure to remove, especially in a competitive race where whoever pauses falls behind. You could have very consequential capability jumps happening faster than anyone can evaluate them, let alone govern them. That's why I think it matters to have visibility into when labs are approaching that point, and some coordination so no single actor feels forced to hit the accelerator blindly.

r002.rationale: It says automating AI research removes the skilled-human bottleneck, allows many faster-than-human copies to work continuously, and shortens improvement cycles.

r003.rationale: It says that once one system matches a top researcher, more copies can simply be run, limited mainly by compute.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the key thing is what happens when AI gets good enough to do AI research itself. Right now the bottleneck on progress isn't compute, it's the number of really strong researchers. There are maybe a few thousand people in the world who can push the frontier. If you can run tens of thousands of copies of an AI that's roughly as good as a top researcher, and they run faster than humans, don't sleep, and can be duplicated, you've effectively multiplied the research labor force by orders of magnitude almost overnight.

And the thing that makes it explosive rather than just fast is the feedback. Each improvement makes the systems better at producing the next improvement. You get a loop that's compounding, not linear. Historically, technologies didn't do that. A better steam engine didn't design the next steam engine. Here the output feeds directly back into the input.

A few things would make it particularly sharp. One is if the improvements are mostly algorithmic rather than needing new hardware. If you need to build new fabs and data centers, that's a physical bottleneck that takes years. But if the gains come from better training methods, better architectures, better data curation, then you can iterate on the timescale of experiments, which could be days or hours. Another is if the systems are good at the full stack, not just coding but forming hypotheses, designing experiments, and interpreting the results. If humans are still in the loop making the judgment calls, that slows things down a lot. Once they're not, the pace is set by the machines.

And there's a geopolitical dimension. If one actor gets a lead on this, even a few months, the compounding means that lead could become decisive. That's part of why I think of this as a national security issue, not just a research question. You get something like a superweapon dynamic, where the incentive to race is enormous, and the incentive to cut corners on safety is enormous too. So the explosiveness isn't just technical. It's that the structure creates pressure to go as fast as possible precisely when you'd most want to be careful.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is when AI can automate AI research itself. You’re no longer just making a system better at some external task; you’re making it better at the process that produces the next system. So you get a feedback loop: better AI does better research, and that research produces even better AI.

What could make that particularly explosive is that you can run many copies in parallel. Human researchers take years to train, and coordinating large groups is difficult. With AI, you could potentially copy a strong researcher, give those copies different experiments, and share the results very quickly. Algorithmic improvements could also make those researchers cheaper to run, allowing you to run more of them.

But a feedback loop doesn’t automatically imply an explosion. Experiments still take time, compute is limited, and research could hit diminishing returns. The question is whether improvements help remove those bottlenecks fast enough that each round of research becomes substantially faster than the last.

r002.rationale: It describes AI copies conducting research and a faster feedback loop, but does not clearly state that removing humans from the recursive development loop enables improvement to proceed at machine speed.

r003.rationale: It says strong AI researchers could potentially be copied, but does not claim that replication would be technologically feasible once human-level AI researchers exist.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key thing is when AI starts improving the process of AI research itself. Right now, even if you have a lot of compute, you still have bottlenecks in figuring out which experiments to run, interpreting the results, and coming up with better algorithms. If you can automate those steps, then a better system can help you build an even better system, which can do that research faster still.

What could make that particularly explosive is the combination of algorithmic improvements and parallelization. You might find an efficiency improvement that lets you run many more copies of your researcher, and those copies can then search for further improvements. And unlike human researchers, they can potentially share what they learn very quickly.

But a feedback loop doesn’t automatically mean an explosion. Experiments take time, compute is limited, and the next improvement might be harder to find. The question is whether improvements increase research capacity fast enough to overcome those bottlenecks. That’s where I think a lot of the uncertainty is.

r002.rationale: It says automated research could proceed faster and that systems may share discoveries quickly, but does not clearly say removing humans from the loop enables machine-speed improvement.

r003.rationale: It mentions copies of a researcher, but does not claim that human-level AI researchers would be technologically feasible to replicate.
